findings.passage: That is the register Olah reaches for. His word for disappointment, across a decade of interviews, is "sad."
findings.problem: The 'sad' lexicon is a load-bearing discriminator (H2 answer, 'Why not Type 6?', FAQ) but it is selectively counted and overstated. (a) Every cited instance is 2021-2026, five years, not 'a decade' (the evidence record itself says 'from 2021 to 2026'). (b) The same transcripts carry fear/worry vocabulary at equal or greater frequency that the draft does not count: in S02 Olah says 'I feel kind of worried about us deploying systems', 'I'm worried this is a pretty serious issue', 'the reason why I'm worried about it isn't even so much the probability... but that it's so invisible'; in S01 'It was just a really scary time period'. The draft even paraphrases that last line as 'what bothered him was not so much the probability', replacing his word 'worried' in the section arguing his word is 'sad'. (c) The 2024 'sort of sad' about hidden-camera gadgets is an aside immediately followed by 'but I was kind of delighted', not a disappointment register. (d) 'Rarely angry, rarely suspicious' sits beside his own 'There was a lot of outrage' and 'really outraged at just the appalling ethics of it'. A word-frequency claim that ignores the counter-words is an attractive story, not a discriminator.
findings.acceptance_test: 'a decade' is gone or replaced by the true span (2021-2026). The AI-suffering paraphrase uses his word 'worried' (or quotes it). Either the frequency argument is dropped as a discriminator, or it is presented beside the worry/scared/outrage instances from the same sources with an explicit statement of why 'sad' still weighs more. 'Rarely angry, rarely suspicious' is removed or reconciled with the two outrage quotes. The FAQ line 'his habitual word for disappointment is "sad," not alarmed' matches the revised body.

findings.passage: Both sides of the typing question are in that answer. Wanting to trust institutions is a Six's sentence. Setting the outrage aside as one hat and landing on sadness is a Four's habit.
findings.problem: Context inversion. In the S01 transcript, the sentence immediately before the quoted trust line is Olah's own statement of where he lands: 'I don't know, where I wind up is something like, just being really disappointed. Because I really want to be able to trust these organizations, and they clearly are systematically falling short.' He also says he has 'gradually had more sympathy also for national security-type concerns'. The hats sentence then holds outrage and sadness in parallel ('one hat... the other hat'); it does not set outrage aside. So by his own words, his resting point is disappointment grounded in wanting to trust institutions, which is the half the draft scores for Six. Calling sadness the 'landing' reverses the source to score a Four point.
findings.acceptance_test: The passage quotes or accurately paraphrases 'where I wind up is something like, just being really disappointed. Because I really want to be able to trust these organizations', and no sentence claims he sets outrage aside or lands on sadness. The answer is scored as mixed or Six-leaning, or its use as Four evidence is dropped. C12's inference in the evidence record is updated to match.

findings.passage: The Six evidence also clusters in real danger (a police raid, frontier AI risk, a Vatican stage) and in professional speech, where fear is reasonable on its face. The Four evidence comes from his private life, across years, in his own words.
findings.problem: This partition is false, and it hides omitted adverse evidence. (1) The draft's own Six paragraph cites private-life items: the dating doc's anxiety, 'not being good enough and my partner leaving me', and the 2020 'alone forever' fear. (2) The dating doc (S04), the draft's central Four exhibit, also says 'Partner was poly, I was anxiously attached' and 'My partner valued spontaneity and adventure, but I found this anxiety producing (especially when adventure involved things that were mildly dangerous).' Neither line appears in the draft or anywhere in evidence-draft.json. They are relational, non-professional, non-danger security signals (anxious attachment; anxiety about mild physical risk), exactly the kind the discriminator says is missing. (3) The 'private life' Four evidence is public tweets and a document written to attract a partner, which the draft itself concedes later. The Six evidence is discounted for context while the Four evidence is not discounted for the same thing.
findings.acceptance_test: Claims for 'anxiously attached' and 'found this anxiety producing (especially when adventure involved things that were mildly dangerous)' are added to the evidence record with S04 locators, and 'Why not Type 6?' confronts them directly. The clustering sentence is deleted or rewritten so it does not say Six evidence is confined to danger or professional speech. Any discount for performance or audience (prepared speech, employer messaging) is applied equally to the dating doc and the threads.

findings.passage: And the shape is the courtroom again. Frightened, then present, then saying the uncomfortable thing out loud. Take the Vatican out of his story and the argument above still stands.
findings.problem: The draft calls the courtroom choice 'a textbook counterphobic Six' (fear, then moving toward the danger). It then finds the same fear-approach-speak sequence at the Vatican 16 years later. That makes it the most consistent cross-context behavior in the record, and by the draft's own definition it is a Six pattern. 'So why does Four lead?' never answers it; it pivots to the longing/dating-doc evidence. Then the Vatican section uses the courtroom echo to neutralize the Vatican as Six evidence. That is circular: a repeated pattern the article labeled Six is treated as a reason to discount Six. The hook ('Fear came first. Then he walked toward the thing that scared him.') foregrounds the same pattern, so the reader is set up for an answer the article never delivers.
findings.acceptance_test: 'Why not Type 6?' explicitly addresses the fear-then-approach pattern (2010 courtroom, 2026 Vatican). Either it gives a sourced Four-specific reading, for example his own stated rationale about not letting someone be 'abandoned' (the 'stepping away... abandoning' quote) as identification with the outcast rather than security-seeking, or it concedes the pattern as unresolved Six evidence. The sentence implying the Vatican's shape weakens the Six case is removed.

findings.passage: About his own central bet he sounds nothing like a doubter: "I'm probably slightly delusionally optimistic about it," he said in 2021
findings.problem: Context stripped. In S02 this is one answer to Wiblin's question about what keeps him up at night 'if you weren't as optimistic of a person'. It opens 'the scaling one is probably the thing that I'm most scared of', continues 'I think there's still a lot of room for things to fail. And I'm the person who should be the most...', and only then says 'slightly delusionally optimistic'. The phrase is a self-skeptical caveat that his optimism may be biased because he leads the agenda, which is doubt about his own judgment. The draft splits the one answer: 'most scared of' goes into the Six column and 'delusionally optimistic' is used to say he 'sounds nothing like a doubter'.
findings.acceptance_test: The optimism quote is presented with the fear clause and the 'room for things to fail' caveat from the same answer, or it is no longer used as evidence against Six. 'sounds nothing like a doubter' is removed or supported by a source whose context does not contain the doubt.

findings.passage: The friend everyone else stepped away from
findings.problem: The heading distorts the source in the direction of the thesis (the lone outsider). In S01 Olah says 'I didn't know him that well, I knew him a bit through HackLab, but a lot of us really rallied in supporting him.' His community rallied; 'everyone else' did not step away. His own principle is about when 'certain people' step away. The body correctly says 'Olah only knew him a bit', but the heading, the description ('support a friend accused of terrorism') and the Type 6 FAQ ('when police raided a friend') call him a friend without noting that 'friend' is Olah's later 2022 shorthand. This involves a criminal accusation against a third party, so the relationship and support framing should be precise.
findings.acceptance_test: The heading no longer claims everyone else stepped away; it matches 'a lot of us really rallied'. Wherever metadata calls the man a 'friend', it either uses language consistent with 'I knew him a bit through HackLab' or attributes 'friend' to Olah's 2022 doc. The body still notes that others in HackLab rallied too.

findings.passage: What would change this read is named colleagues saying that, under stress at work, he habitually seeks reassurance, defers to authority or expects the worst. The research for this page found no such account.
findings.problem: Asymmetric absence-of-evidence. The evidence record lists this colleague testimony as an open research task, not a completed search with a negative result. It also notes that no named colleague describes moodiness, self-absorption, envy or withdrawal either. The draft reports the absence only on the Six side, so the gap reads as support for Four. Combined with medium confidence and contested_typing in the evidence record, the flat type statements ('Chris Olah's personality type is Enneagram Type 4, the Individualist.' in the H2 answer and FAQ, '(Enneagram Type 4)' in the title) state more certainty than the record holds.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence states that no named colleague testimony was found in either direction (no reassurance-seeking, and no moodiness or withdrawal). The H2 answer and type FAQ mark Four as the best-supported read with Six close (for example 'most likely' or 'best fit'), stay within 60 words, and keep the rest of the article free of extra hedging.

findings.passage: None of these overturns the read. Together they describe a Four who is gentler, more orderly and more optimistic than the type's reputation, and who meets his own sadness with a statistics joke as often as a poem.
findings.problem: Five items of counterevidence (agreeableness, Two-like kindness, systematizing, scrupulosity, curated self-presentation) are dismissed in one unargued sentence and then folded into a redefinition of the type. That is the 'explain away every contradiction' move the standard warns against. The evidence record's 'unexplained' list (including the absence of any outside account of moodiness or envy) is not represented as unexplained. The agreeableness paragraph says 'Nines and some Sixes' fit better, but Nine is never tested.
findings.acceptance_test: The closing names at least one item the Four reading does not explain (consistent with the evidence record's 'unexplained' field) rather than reframing all of it as type flavor. Nine gets a sourced sentence on why it fails, or the 'Nines' mention is removed. The line can stay warm, but it must not claim the counterevidence is absorbed without saying how.

protected_passages.passage: The bullying isn't offered here as the cause of his type; the sources describe the experience, not what it did to him.
protected_passages.reason: Explicit refusal of the attractive childhood-wound causal story; exactly the inference limit the standard asks for.

protected_passages.passage: The Six case is strong. Fear came first in his defining crisis, by his own account.
protected_passages.reason: Opens the rival case as a genuine steelman with his own words, not a strawman; keep the full paragraph's breadth (anxiety, outside backing, 'safe person', Vatican plea).

protected_passages.reason: The most distinctive, verified, person-specific detail in the piece, including his owned envy through the pastor; this is the strongest Four exhibit and is quoted faithfully.

protected_passages.reason: Honest discount on the article's own favorite evidence; the self-presentation caveat that follows should be preserved and applied evenly (see critic-F3).

assessment: A well-sourced, unusually honest draft. The quotations I reopened (80,000 Hours #107 and #108, the dating doc, the Lex transcript) are accurate word for word, and it steelmans Type 6 seriously. The weakness is in how adverse evidence is weighed, not in whether it is quoted. Three Four-side arguments read their sources against context: the 'sad' word count ignores equally frequent 'worried'/'scared'/'outrage' (F1), the security-agencies answer drops his own 'where I wind up' sentence (F2), and the optimism quote is cut from the 'most scared of' answer it sits in (F5). The 'Six evidence is situational, Four evidence is private' partition is false, and it hides two omitted Six-leaning lines from the central exhibit, 'anxiously attached' and anxiety about 'mildly dangerous' adventure (F3). The repeated fear-then-approach pattern, which the draft itself calls counterphobic Six, is never answered (F4). Four may still win: his 'abandoning' rationale, the Gilead reading and the dated beauty motive are real. But the margin is narrower than the prose claims, so the type statements should carry the evidence record's medium confidence (F7). The sensitive third-party accusation is handled carefully in the body; the heading and metadata overstate both the friendship and his isolation (F6). Similarity diagnostic: the tripped pairs (mike-faist 0.652, hunter-schafer 0.176) share only standard triad vocabulary ('whose core emotion is shame/fear'), which is ordinary type vocabulary, not reused argument; no finding. Risks: sensitive_allegations (terrorism accusation against an identifiable third party; anonymously sourced Vatican account) and contested_typing (medium confidence, 4 vs 6 close) both stand.
